15496:
Baal-zebub was the god of the Philistine city of Ekron, whom King Ahaziah of Israel tried to consult when he was injured. The name as written means 'Lord of Flies'.

Most scholars think that is a deliberate insult. At Ugarit Baal is often called zbl b'l, 'Prince Baal', so the god's real title was probably Baal-zebul, 'Baal the Prince' or 'Lord of the exalted house'. Changing one letter turned 'Lord Prince' into 'Lord of Flies'. By the time of Jesus 'Beelzebul' had become a name for the prince of demons.
15497: No myth of Ekron's god survives. If he was a local Baal, his worshippers will have told the storm god's stories: Baal the Prince (zbl), who defeats Sea, dies and returns. A minority view takes 'lord of flies' at face value: a god who could drive away (or send) flies and the diseases they carried, comparable to the Greek 'Zeus Apomyios', 'Zeus who averts flies'.
15498:
King Ahaziah of Israel, son of Ahab, falls through the lattice of his upper room in Samaria and sends messengers to ask Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts them with a question that becomes the theme of the story: 'Is it because there is no God in Israel that you are going to inquire of Baal-zebub?' Ahaziah dies as Elijah predicted (2 Kgs 1:2-17).

In the Gospels, opponents accuse Jesus of driving out demons 'by Beelzebul, the prince of demons' (Matt 12:24; Mark 3:22; Luke 11:15). Jesus answers that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand, and that if he casts out demons by the Spirit (finger) of God, the kingdom of God has come. He also says that if they called the master of the house Beelzebul, they will malign his household too (Matt 10:25), which may play on zebul as 'house'. The Greek manuscripts read Beelzeboul; the Latin Vulgate and Syriac tradition read Beelzebub, which is why the KJV has 'Beelzebub'.

15530:
Baal-peor was 'the lord of Peor', a local god worshipped at a mountain shrine in Moab, across the Jordan from Jericho. Israel's first great fall into idolatry, just before entering the promised land, happened there.

The story became a byword. For centuries afterwards prophets, psalmists and apostles remembered 'what happened at Peor' as the warning example of how quickly God's people could abandon him.
15531: Nothing is known of this god apart from the Bible. Most scholars think he was a local form of Baal (or of Chemosh) worshipped at Mount Peor. Psalm 106:28 says Israel 'ate sacrifices offered to the dead', which has led some scholars to link the cult with the marzeah, a feast for the dead known from Ugarit and later texts; others take 'the dead' as a jibe at lifeless idols.
15532:
While Israel camped at Shittim, the people 'began to whore with the daughters of Moab', ate at their sacrificial meals, bowed to their gods and 'yoked themselves to Baal of Peor' (Num 25:1-3). A plague broke out; Phinehas the priest ended it by spearing an Israelite man and a Midianite woman in the act. 24,000 died (Num 25:9; Paul gives 23,000 in 1 Cor 10:8, perhaps counting a single day or using a round figure). Numbers later blames Balaam's advice for the seduction (Num 31:16).

The event became a standard warning: Deut 4:3; Josh 22:17 ('is the iniquity of Peor too little for us?'); Hos 9:10 ('they came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the shame'); Ps 106:28-31; 1 Cor 10:8; Rev 2:14.

Renaissance demonology turned him into Belphegor, a demon of sloth and ingenious invention, the hero of Machiavelli's comic tale *Belfagor arcidiavolo*.

15556:
Baal-berith, 'Lord of the Covenant', was the god of the old Canaanite city of Shechem. After Gideon died, the Israelites 'made Baal-berith their god', and his temple funded the bloody rise of Gideon's son Abimelech.

The name is striking because Shechem was also where Joshua renewed Israel's covenant with Yahweh. So the city had two 'covenant' traditions side by side, and the Bible tells how one was swapped for the other.
15557: No myth survives. He is called both Baal-berith (Judg 8:33; Judg 9:4) and El-berith (Judg 9:46), so scholars debate whether he was a form of El, a form of Baal, or a title used for both. 'Lord of the Covenant' probably means the god who guaranteed treaties sworn in his temple, perhaps a treaty between Shechem's Canaanites and neighbouring Israelite clans.
15558:
Shechem was already an old sacred site in Genesis: Abraham's first altar in Canaan (Gen 12:6-7) and Jacob's purchase of land and altar there (Gen 33:18-20). Joshua made a covenant with Israel at Shechem and set up a great stone under the oak by the sanctuary (Josh 24:25-26).

After Gideon's death, the Israelites again served the Baals and made Baal-berith their god (Judg 8:33). The Shechemites gave Abimelech 70 pieces of silver from Baal-berith's temple, with which he hired 'worthless and reckless men' and murdered his 70 brothers (Judg 9:4-5). When Abimelech later turned on Shechem, about a thousand people took refuge in the stronghold of the temple of El-berith; he set it on fire and they all died (Judg 9:46-49).

15578:
Ptgyh is a goddess known from just one inscription: the royal dedication stone found at Ekron, one of the five Philistine cities, in 1996. The king of Ekron says he built the temple for 'Ptgyh his lady'.

Nobody knows who she was. The Bible never mentions her. She is a useful reminder that the Bible names only a few of the gods its neighbours worshipped, and that archaeology keeps turning up new ones.
15579: No myth is known. Because the Philistines came from the Aegean world, several scholars have proposed that Ptgyh is a Greek goddess written in Semitic letters: suggestions include Pythogaia (an earth goddess linked with Delphi), Potnia ('Lady', a title of Aegean goddesses) or a form of Gaia. None of these is proven.

15582: Ekron is one of the five Philistine cities that received the ark; its later temple belonged to Ptgyh.
15584: David serves Achish king of Gath. The same name (Ikausu) appears centuries later for a king of Ekron in the Ptgyh inscription.

15607:
Molech is the name the Bible links with the worst practice it condemns: making children 'pass through the fire', that is, burning them as sacrifices, at a place called Topheth in the valley just south of Jerusalem.

There is a real scholarly argument about whether Molech was a god at all. The consonants mlk mean 'king'. Many scholars think the vowels were changed to those of bosheth, 'shame', turning melek ('king') into molek. Others, following Otto Eissfeldt (1935), argue that molk was a Phoenician word for a type of sacrifice, so 'to Molech' originally meant 'as a molk-offering'. Others again argue that Molech was a real underworld god. What no one disputes is that the Bible describes child sacrifice in Judah and condemns it in the strongest terms.
15608: No myth of a god called Molech survives. If he was a god, the best candidate is Malik or Milku, a god of the underworld and the dead attested at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit, where one text places 'Milku' at Ashtaroth in Bashan. The famous picture of Moloch as a hollow bronze idol with a bull's head, heated red-hot, with children placed in its arms while drums drowned out the cries, comes from medieval Jewish commentaries (e.g. Rashi on Jer 7:31, explaining the name Topheth from toph, 'drum') and from Greek stories about Carthage, not from the Bible or any ancient Israelite source.
15609:
The law forbids giving any child 'to Molech' on pain of death (Lev 18:21; Lev 20:2-5) and forbids making a child 'pass through the fire' (Deut 18:10). Despite this, two kings of Judah did it: Ahaz 'made his son pass through the fire' (2 Kgs 16:3) and Manasseh did the same (2 Kgs 21:6). Topheth in the Valley of Ben-Hinnom was the site (Jer 7:31; Jer 32:35). God says through Jeremiah that it was something 'I did not command, nor did it come into my mind' (Jer 7:31; Jer 19:5). Josiah defiled Topheth so that no one could use it again (2 Kgs 23:10), probably around 622 BC.

Solomon is said to have built a high place for 'Molech the abomination of the Ammonites' (1 Kgs 11:7), whereas two verses earlier the Ammonite god is Milcom (1 Kgs 11:5). This suggests either that the two names were confused or that the writer treated Milcom and Molech as the same 'king' god.

The Valley of Hinnom (ge hinnom) became, through its association with burning and judgement (Jer 7:32; Jer 19:6), the name Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for the place of final judgement (eleven times in the Gospels, e.g. Matt 5:22; Mark 9:43). Stephen, quoting the Greek of Amos 5:26, mentions 'the tent of Moloch' (Acts 7:43); the Hebrew of Amos reads 'Sakkuth your king' at that point.

15641: Moloch became the archetype of a god who devours children. Milton's *Paradise Lost* (Book 1) puts Moloch first in the catalogue of fallen angels: a horrid king smeared with the blood of human sacrifice and parents' tears, worshipped by the Ammonites with drums drowning the children's cries. In modern culture Moloch stands for any system that consumes people: the machine in Fritz Lang's film *Metropolis* (1927) and the 'Moloch' section of Allen Ginsberg's poem *Howl* (1956).

15657:
Milcom was the national god of the Ammonites, whose capital Rabbah lies under modern Amman in Jordan. His name comes from melek, 'king'. Solomon built him a shrine on the hill east of Jerusalem, which stood until Josiah tore it down.

Because Milcom and Molech share the same root letters, the Bible itself sometimes seems to mix them up, and scholars still debate whether they were one god or two. The best evidence is that Milcom was Ammon's ordinary state god, while 'Molech' is linked mainly with child sacrifice in Jerusalem.
15658: No Ammonite myths survive. Ammonite personal names and seals show a people who worshipped Milcom alongside El and others, much as Moabites worshipped Chemosh and Judahites Yahweh. A national god was the divine king of the land: he gave it to his people and fought their wars.
15659:
Solomon 'went after Milcom the abomination of the Ammonites' and built a high place for him (1 Kgs 11:5; 1 Kgs 11:33); Josiah defiled it centuries later (2 Kgs 23:13). Zephaniah condemns those who swear by Yahweh and also by Milcom (Zeph 1:5, Masoretic 'Malcam'). Jeremiah asks why 'Milcom' has dispossessed Gad and his people settle in its cities, and announces that Milcom will go into exile with his priests (Jer 49:1; Jer 49:3).

When David captured Rabbah he took 'the crown of their king' (malkam), weighing a talent of gold, and it was placed on David's head (2 Sam 12:30). A talent (around 30 kg) is too heavy for a human king to wear, so many (following the Greek Septuagint, which reads 'Milcom their king') think it was the crown of Milcom's statue, perhaps with its precious stone set in David's crown. This is a plausible reading, not a certain one.

1 Kings 11:7 calls the Ammonite god 'Molech', raising the question whether Milcom and Molech were the same. Most scholars now treat them as distinct, explaining 11:7 as a scribal slip or a deliberate slur.
